column2: There is no nobility, so surnames carry no prefix and are ordinary ones.
Noble houses place "von" before the surname (e.g. von Kleist). The imperial family uses the nation's name, Ragnar, as its surname, and commoners use surnames without a prefix.
Noble houses place "de" before the surname (e.g. de Valois). The royal family uses the nation's name, Edrein, as its surname, and commoners use surnames without a prefix.
Noble houses place "van" before the surname (e.g. van Klein). The royal family uses the nation's name, Bersel, as its surname, and commoners use surnames without a prefix.

Noble houses place "di" before the surname (e.g. di Moretti). The royal family uses the nation's name, Seradium, as its surname, and commoners use surnames without a prefix. The saint, though not a noble, takes "di" as an exception.
There is no nobility, so there is no prefix, and surnames are drawn from forests and nature (e.g. Oak, Pine, Willow).

On campus, uniforms are worn neatly. The black ribbon is tied in a bow just below the collar, and a small jeweled brooch is pinned at the knot. The brooch's gem color is the symbol color of the student's faculty; it is a faculty marker, not a magic tool.
White shirt, white skirt, black corset with gold buttons, black ribbon, navy cloak with gold piping, jeweled brooch
White shirt, white pants, silver belt, black ribbon, navy jacket with gold piping, jeweled brooch
Freshmen wear the uniform without a brooch until the entrance ceremony, where their assigned instructor awards them their faculty's brooch.
